\section[pēr]{\ml{പേര്} (pēru) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} the native Dravidian word}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-peru}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Name\textquotedblright{} — native, as you'd expect from Tamil's closest sister.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Malayalam.)} \textbf{\ml{പ}} (pa) + \textbf{\ml{േ}} (the \emph{ē}-sign) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{പേ}} (pē); \textbf{\ml{ര്}} (bare \emph{r}, chandrakkala). Read \textbf{\ml{പേ}·\ml{ര്}} $\to$ \textbf{pēru}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പേര്}} (\emph{pēru}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{native Dravidian}, from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pēr} — the same word as Tamil \emph{peyar} and Telugu \emph{pēru}, a cousin of Kannada \emph{hesaru} (\emph{p}$\to$\emph{h}). Being Tamil's closest sister, Malayalam keeps the native word, \emph{not} Sanskrit \emph{nāma} (Hindi \emph{nām}, English \emph{name}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pēru\textquotedblright{}
  \item its cousins — \emph{pēru} / \emph{peyar} / \emph{pēr} / \emph{hesaru}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\ml{പേര്}} native or borrowed, and what Tamil word is its twin? (Native Dravidian, \emph{*pēr}; Tamil \emph{peyar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[ē]{\ml{◌േ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S134-vowel-sign-ee}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{പ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌േ}}
\textbf{\ml{◌േ}} — \emph{ē}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ē}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Look at \textbf{\ml{പേര്}} again. The \textbf{\ml{പ}} you read on the page before carries an \emph{a} of its own — \emph{pa}. The hook standing in front of it, \textbf{\ml{േ}}, takes that \emph{a} away and puts a long \emph{ē} in its place: \emph{pa} $\to$ \emph{pē}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{പേര്}} \emph{pēr} — name
\end{itemize}

Malayalam prints this sign to the LEFT of its consonant even though the vowel is pronounced AFTER it. Your eye reads it first; your mouth says it second.

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{◌േ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{◌േ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\section[ṟa]{\ml{റ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṟ}, it is \textbf{ṟa}.

Malayalam has two \emph{r} letters. \textbf{\ml{ര}} is the soft one you have been reading inside \textbf{\ml{നമസ്കാരം}} and \textbf{\ml{ശരി}}. \textbf{\ml{റ}} is the hard one, made further forward in the mouth — and it is the one hiding inside your new word.

\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{എന്റെ}} \emph{enṟe} — my
\end{itemize}

Here \textbf{\ml{റ}} sits underneath \textbf{\ml{ന}} as the stacked pair \textbf{\ml{ന്റ}}, which is why it does not announce itself at first. Find its curl in the lower half.

\section[āṇŭ]{\ml{ആണ്} (āṇŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} where Malayalam breaks with its sisters}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-aanu}



\begin{quote}
A small surprise: Malayalam has a real word for \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} where its Dravidian sisters have none.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Malayalam.)} \textbf{\ml{ആ}} (independent long \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\ml{ണ്}} (bare retroflex \emph{ṇ}) $\to$ \textbf{āṇŭ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} (\emph{āṇŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) is Malayalam's \textbf{copula} — a real \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} word, grown from the verb \textbf{\ml{ആക}} (\emph{āka}, \textquotedblleft{}to be, to become\textquotedblright{}).

Here's the point: Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu all use the \textbf{zero copula} — \emph{no} word for \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{} Yet Malayalam, though it is Tamil's \emph{closest} sister, grammaticalised a \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} verb. So where Tamil says only \emph{eṉ peyar Arun}, Malayalam adds \emph{āṇŭ}: \emph{enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb comes last}]
Like Hindi's \emph{hai} (and unlike Tamil), \emph{āṇŭ} closes the sentence — Malayalam is subject–object–\textbf{verb}: \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun \textbf{is}.\textquotedblright{} (Malayalis sometimes drop \emph{āṇŭ} in fast speech, but the full form keeps it.)
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}āṇŭ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the contrast — Tamil \emph{eṉ peyar Arun} (no verb) vs. Malayalam \emph{enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{athe}, then say \emph{illa}, then read \textbf{\ml{ശരി}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}, and how does Malayalam differ from Tamil here? (The copula \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{āka}; Malayalam \emph{has} a word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} where Tamil uses none.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[enṟe pēru … āṇŭ]{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} … \ml{ആണ്} (enṟe pēru … āṇŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-enre-peru-aanu}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the three atoms — including the copula \emph{āṇŭ} that Tamil lacks.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item enṟe (my) + pēru (name) + your name + āṇŭ (is).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} … \ml{ആണ്}} = \textquotedblleft{}my name … is\textquotedblright{} = \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\emph{Enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: verb last}]
Malayalam is subject–object–\textbf{verb}, so \emph{āṇŭ} (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) sits at the end — \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun \textbf{is},\textquotedblright{} like Hindi \emph{hai} and unlike Tamil's verbless \emph{eṉ peyar Arun}.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[nī / niṅṅaḷ]{\ml{നീ} / \ml{നിങ്ങൾ} (nī / niṅṅaḷ) — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} familiar and respectful}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-nii-ningal}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}You\textquotedblright{} — respect made by the plural, the family's shared trick.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Malayalam.)} \textbf{\ml{നീ}} (\emph{nī}); \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} (\emph{niṅṅaḷ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{നീ}} (\emph{nī}, familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*nīn} — the same native root as Tamil \emph{nī}, Kannada \emph{nīnu}, Telugu \emph{nuvvu}. \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} (\emph{niṅṅaḷ}) is the respectful/plural \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nī} + a plural ending, the exact cousin of Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: respect by the plural}]
\emph{nī} (familiar) vs. \emph{niṅṅaḷ} (respectful, literally plural) — the family's shared politeness-by-plural, same idea as French \emph{vous}. For a first meeting, \textbf{niṅṅaḷ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}nī\textquotedblright{} (familiar), \textquotedblleft{}niṅṅaḷ\textquotedblright{} (respectful)
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ml{പേര്}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Malayalam make \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} respectful, and which Tamil word is \emph{niṅṅaḷ}'s twin? (By the plural; Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ī]{\ml{◌ീ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S138-vowel-sign-ii}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ണ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌ീ}}
\textbf{\ml{◌ീ}} — \emph{ī}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ī}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Look at \textbf{\ml{നീ}}. The \textbf{\ml{ന}} you already read carries an \emph{a}; the sign hanging off its right, \textbf{\ml{◌ീ}}, replaces that \emph{a} with a long \emph{ī}: \emph{na} $\to$ \emph{nī}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നീ}} \emph{nī} — you (familiar)
\end{itemize}

It is the long partner of the small hook you have been reading at the end of \textbf{\ml{നന്ദി}} and \textbf{\ml{ശരി}}; that one is short \emph{i}, this one is held.

Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\section[ḷ]{\ml{ൾ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S06-letter-chillu-ll}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{◌ീ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ൾ}}
\textbf{\ml{ൾ}} — \emph{ḷ}.

It is a \textbf{chillu} — a consonant with its vowel stripped away and given a shape of its own, so that it can end a word without a dangling mark.

You have already said a word that ends with it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} \emph{niṅṅaḷ} — you (respectful)
\end{itemize}

Every consonant in this script arrives carrying an \emph{a}. A word that ends in a bare consonant therefore needs a way to say \textquotedblleft{}no vowel here.\textquotedblright{} Malayalam gives a handful of consonants a special end-of-word shape called a \textbf{chillu}, and \textbf{\ml{ൾ}} is the chillu of the retroflex \emph{ḷ}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ൾ} — copy what you see}

Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\section[entŭ]{\ml{എന്ത്} (entŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-entu}



\begin{quote}
The last piece of the question: \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Malayalam.)} \textbf{\ml{എ}} (\emph{e}) + the conjunct \textbf{\ml{ന്ത്}} (\emph{ntŭ}) $\to$ \textbf{entŭ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}} (\emph{entŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, on the interrogative stem \textbf{*yā-/*e-} — the same Dravidian question-root as Tamil \emph{eṉṉa} and Telugu \emph{ēmiṭi}, heading Malayalam's question family: \emph{entŭ} (what), \emph{ār} (who), \emph{eviṭe} (where).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}entŭ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the question family — entŭ, ār, eviṭe
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{enṟe}, then read \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Dravidian stem heads \textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}}? (\emph{*yā-/*e-}, same as Tamil \emph{eṉṉa}, Telugu \emph{ēmiṭi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?]{\ml{നിന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} \ml{എന്താണ്}? (ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-ninre-peru-entaanu}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the question — your + name + what-is. And notice the copula hiding in the last word.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നിന്റെ}} (\emph{ninṟe}, \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) = the possessive of \emph{nī} (\textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{\ml{എന്താണ്}} (\emph{entāṇŭ}) = \textbf{entŭ} (what) + \textbf{āṇŭ} (is), fused into one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{നിന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} \ml{എന്താണ്}?} = literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your name what is?}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Unlike the Tamil question (which had \textbf{no} verb), Malayalam carries its copula \emph{āṇŭ} right inside the question-word \emph{entāṇŭ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answer, and the respectful version}]
Answer with the sentence you built: \textbf{Enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ.} The respectful \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} is \emph{niṅṅaḷuṭe}: \emph{niṅṅaḷuṭe pēru entāṇŭ?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item hear the copula inside — \emph{entŭ} + \emph{āṇŭ} $\to$ \emph{entāṇŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words fuse into \textbf{\ml{എന്താണ്}}, and how does this differ from the Tamil question? (\emph{entŭ} \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} + \emph{āṇŭ} \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}; Tamil's question has no verb, Malayalam's carries the copula.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[santōṣam]{\ml{സന്തോഷം} (santōṣam) — \textquotedblleft{}joy,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-santosham}



\begin{quote}
The warm close — a Sanskrit word even in native-loving Malayalam.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the words you can use}
\textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} (\emph{santōṣam}) literally means \textquotedblleft{}joy.\textquotedblright{} At the end of a short introduction, it can stand by itself for \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you.\textquotedblright{} A fuller phrase exists, but it needs words and grammar you have not learned yet; the one-word version is complete and useful now.

\subsection*{Script: two new shapes to notice}
Keep \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} visible. Most of its shapes have already appeared in this chapter. Point to just two new ones:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഷ}} carries the \emph{ṣa} sound near the end.
  \item \textbf{\ml{ോ}} is the long \emph{ō} vowel sign attached to the consonant before it.
\end{itemize}

Look, point, and say the whole word once. The next two-minute lesson will let your hand copy it with the model still present.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} (\emph{santōṣam}, \textquotedblleft{}joy\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{Sanskrit} — the same loan Kannada and Telugu use. So even Malayalam, the great keeper of native words (recall \emph{nandi} for \textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{} in Chapter 1), reaches for Sanskrit here. The loanwords spread \textbf{selectively}, word by word — which is exactly what these cognate notes trace: native for \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}thanks,\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit for \textquotedblleft{}pleased.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}santōṣam\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pattern — Malayalam keeps native \emph{nandi} (thanks) but borrows Sanskrit \emph{santōṣam} (pleased)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} native or Sanskrit, and what does that show about how Malayalam borrows? (Sanskrit; it borrows \emph{selectively} — native for some words, Sanskrit for others.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — the introduction, whole}

\label{lesson:ML-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole introduction, in the order two people actually say it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Malayalam} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} \ml{മീരാ} \ml{ആണ്}. (\emph{enṟe pēru Mira āṇŭ}) & My name is Mira. \\
\ml{നിന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} \ml{എന്താണ്}? (\emph{ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ}) & What's your name? \\
\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} \ml{അരുൺ} \ml{ആണ്}. (\emph{enṟe pēru Arun āṇŭ}) & My name is Arun. \\
\ml{സന്തോഷം}. (\emph{santōṣam}) & Pleased to meet you. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every atom traced:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pēru} $\leftarrow$ Dravidian \emph{*pēr} (\emph{not} \emph{name}; twin of Tamil \emph{peyar})
  \item \textbf{enṟe} — the native Dravidian possessive \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{āṇŭ} $\leftarrow$ the verb \emph{āka} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}) — Malayalam's \textbf{copula}
  \item \textbf{entŭ} $\leftarrow$ Dravidian question-stem \emph{*yā-/*e-}
  \item \textbf{santōṣam} $\leftarrow$ \textbf{Sanskrit} (borrowed even in native-loving Malayalam)
\end{itemize}

The Malayalam standout: unlike its Dravidian sisters' \textbf{zero copula}, Malayalam \textbf{has a word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}} (\emph{āṇŭ}) — a real grammatical difference between the closest of sisters.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item your own introduction — \textquotedblleft{}enṟe pēru … āṇŭ\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask it back — \textquotedblleft{}ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing check — keep the model visible}
Keep the dialogue table open. Copy \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} once from its visible row, then compare your two new shapes, \textbf{\ml{ഷ}} and \textbf{\ml{ോ}}, with the model. This is supported checkpoint writing, not spelling from memory.

\subsection*{Script check — the letters of this chapter}
Cover the romanizations. Find each letter once in the Malayalam above, then say the word it sits in.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{പേര്}} — \textbf{\ml{പ}} \emph{pa}, \textbf{\ml{◌േ}} \emph{ē}
  \item \textbf{\ml{എന്റെ}} — \textbf{\ml{എ}} \emph{e}, \textbf{\ml{റ}} \emph{ṟa}
  \item \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} — \textbf{\ml{ആ}} \emph{ā}, \textbf{\ml{ണ}} \emph{ṇa}
  \item \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} — \textbf{\ml{◌ീ}} \emph{ī} (in \textbf{\ml{നീ}}), \textbf{\ml{ൾ}} \emph{ḷ}
  \item \textbf{\ml{അരുൺ}} — \textbf{\ml{◌ു}} \emph{u}, \textbf{\ml{ൺ}} \emph{ṇ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at each letter, then find it in the word beside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name, ask someone else's, say you're pleased. (\emph{Enṟe pēru … āṇŭ. / Ninṟe pēru entāṇŭ? / Santōṣam.}) What grammatical word does Malayalam have that Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu lack? (A copula — \emph{āṇŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{})
